name: Micro-expressions

card.summary: Fleeting involuntary facial expressions lasting under half a second, studied for reading emotion and used by people who want to improve their expressiveness and read faces.
card.note: Lie-detection claims about micro-expressions are disputed by researchers.

quick.overview:
A micro-expression is a very brief facial expression, usually under half a second, that flashes across the face when someone has an emotion they are trying to hide or suppress. The idea goes back to Haggard and Isaacs in 1966 and was developed by Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen.

In looksmaxxing and social-skills circles it relates to how the face communicates: people interested in charisma and face reading study expressions to come across as warmer and to read others. Training tools exist, and researchers also build computer-vision systems to detect micro-expressions.
quick.how: People use video training tools such as the micro and subtle facial expression training tools, which present clips and give feedback, and some practise expression in a mirror or on camera.
quick.risks: There are no physical risks. Researchers dispute how well micro-expressions reveal deception, and critics warn against using them to judge suspects or strangers.

lead: A micro-expression is a brief facial expression, typically lasting under half a second, produced when voluntary and involuntary emotional responses conflict so that a true feeling shows briefly before a false one replaces it.[1] Haggard and Isaacs first described "micro-momentary" expressions in 1966 while scanning psychotherapy films, and Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen later found agreement on emotion labels across cultures, including among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea in 1971.[1]

Expression is one part of how a face is perceived. Interest in micro-expressions is mainly about emotional signalling and social perception rather than facial structure. Training tools called MFETT and SFETT are used to improve recognition, often with people who find social situations difficult.[1]
Researchers have questioned the lie-detection claims. A 2008 study that coded 700 expressions found only 2% were micro-expressions, appearing equally in truth-tellers and liars.[1]

chain: Learn how emotion shows on the face
Expressions become more deliberate and natural
angle.text: People study micro-expressions to understand how emotion shows on the face and to improve their own expression and social reading. It concerns expression, not bone structure.

paras: Wikipedia distinguishes simulated, neutralized and masked micro-expressions: a flash of expression over a neutral face, a suppressed genuine emotion, and a genuine emotion covered by a fake one.[1] Ekman's seven universal emotions are disgust, anger, fear, sadness, happiness, contempt and surprise.[1]

Reported lie-detection accuracy averages about 54% for ordinary people and 64% for Secret Service agents, with Ekman-linked cohorts reaching 68-73%.[1] Critics including Maria Hartwig argue that reliance on such cues has contributed to wrongful imprisonment of aggressively interrogated suspects, and a 2016 Scientific Reports study found people fail to tell real from masked expressions over 40% of the time.[1]
Computer scientists have built datasets and recognition systems for automatic micro-expression analysis, with surveys covering databases, methods and challenges.[2][3]
The 2009 TV series Lie to Me was based on Ekman's work.[1] A 2015 Hacker News thread discussed airport behaviour-detection screening said to look for micro-expressions.[6]

Studies include a pilot of micro-expression recognition training in medical students,[4] a pilot of emotion-recognition remediation in schizophrenia using a micro-expression training tool,[5] and technical surveys of recognition datasets and algorithms.[2][3]

timeline.event: Haggard and Isaacs identify micro-momentary expressions.[1]
Ekman and Friesen report cross-cultural agreement on emotion labels.[1]
Porter and ten Brinke coding study of 700 expressions.[1]
